newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to revamp industry and woo foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Albania to revamp industry and woo foreigners.

text.p: Albania, desperate to resuscitate its ravaged economy after months of anarchy, plans a dramatic restructuring of key industries to attract foreign investment, the government's economic minister said in an interview.

Ylli Bufi, given the tough job of sprucing up and privatising the Balkan nation's depleted assets, told Reuters a concrete strategy on developing and selling off the main holdings would be presented to parliament next month.
"We will improve the managing of state holdings in oil, mining, electricity and other sectors to make them more flexible so that we can speed up the process of privatisation," he said.

The World Bank and other key donors have already worked out an extensive programme which would help deliver the country from an economic abyss and open the way to large-scale investment from foreign institutions.

The international community, which helped Albania stage elections after protests at collapsed "get-rich-quick" investment schemes degenerated into violence, has pledged social, economic and military aid to Europe's poorest nation.
The International Monetary Fund said longer-term loans could also be negotiated, but laid down conditions which the government in Tirana would first have to meet.

These include improving security by bringing the whole country under government control, building up a satisfactory record of tax collection, winding up pyramid schemes and reducing the budget deficit.

The months of unrest, which claimed more than 1,500 lives in the former hermitic communist country, have left much of Albania's enterprises in a deplorable state. Factories stand inert, some on the brink of liquidation or already bankrupt.

The new Socialist-led government, voted in by a huge majority after the fall of former president Sali Berisha's Democrats, has vowed to start restructuring Europe's poorhouse by reforming the police, the army and the financial system.
Traditionally the bulk of Albania's exports were half-made clothing and shoes. Other sources of foreign currency were medicinal plants, electricity and minerals -- notably chromium and copper ore.
"There are many possibilities for the oil, chromium and copper industries because of the reserves. But they need to be reorganised after years of complete idleness and bureaucracy," Bufi said.
Albania now aims to focus on raising oil production by around 30 percent and chromium production above last year's 240,000 tonnes.

"The copper industry is almost in total collapse. The electricity industry is in a better state but needs investment and restructuring as losses in the network are big and consumers' money is not being collected very well," Bufi said.
The minister said gross domestic product (GDP), which had risen 9.1 percent in 1996, was expected to plummet seven percent this year to stand at around 415 billion leks ($2.4 billion).
To kick-start the economy Bufi plans to resume production in major enterprises with the offer of short-term loans, and to make them more efficient and competitive.
"Their assets, which make up 80 percent of public property, yield less than 30 percent of GDP," he said.
Despite inheriting an economy in shambles, the minister is convinced he can stabilise the economy this year and put the country into the fast lane of development and economic growth next year.
"If we fail in our reform it will have grave consequences for the nation and that is why we are being very prudent not to make their (previous government's) mistakes," Bufi said.
